title: Chapter 17 — Principal Causes Maintaining The Democratic Republic In The United States
paragraphs: Principal Causes Which Tend to Maintain the Democratic Republic in the United States

A democratic republic exists in the United States, and the main purpose of this book has been to explain why it exists. As my subject carried me along, I passed over several of the causes that help sustain the institutions of America, or only hinted at them. Others I have been unable to discuss. And those I have dwelt on most are, so to speak, buried in the details of the earlier parts of this work. So before I go on to speak of the future, I think the best thing I can do is to gather into a small space the reasons that best explain the present. In this chapter I look back, and I shall be brief. I shall only remind the reader, in the briefest way, of what he already knows, and I shall select only the most prominent of the facts I have not yet pointed out.
All the causes that help maintain the democratic republic in the United States can be reduced to three heads:—
I. The unusual and accidental situation in which Providence has placed the Americans.
III. The manners and customs of the people.

Accidental or Providential Causes Which Contribute to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States The Union has no neighbors — No metropolis — The Americans have had the chances of birth in their favor — America an empty country — How this circumstance contributes powerfully to the maintenance of the democratic republic in America — How the American wilds are peopled — Avidity of the Anglo-Americans in taking possession of the solitudes of the New World — Influence of physical prosperity upon the political opinions of the Americans.

A thousand circumstances, independent of human will, combine to make it easier to maintain a democratic republic in the United States. Some of these peculiarities are well known, and the others can easily be pointed out. But I shall limit myself to the most prominent among them.

The Americans have no neighbors, and so they have no great wars, financial crises, invasions, or conquests to fear. They need neither heavy taxes nor large armies nor great generals. And they have nothing to fear from a scourge more dangerous to republics than all these evils together: military glory. It is impossible to deny the immense influence that military glory has on the spirit of a nation. General Jackson, whom the Americans have twice elected to head their government, has a violent temper and mediocre talents. Nothing in the whole course of his career ever showed that he is qualified to govern a free people, and indeed the majority of the educated classes of the Union has always opposed him. Yet he was raised to the Presidency, and has been kept in that high position, solely by the memory of a victory he won twenty years ago under the walls of New Orleans. That victory, however, was a very ordinary achievement, and it could only be remembered in a country where battles are rare. And the people that is carried away in this manner by the illusions of glory is unquestionably the coldest and most calculating, the least military (if I may use the expression), and the most prosaic of all the peoples on earth.

America has no great capital city *a whose influence is felt, directly or indirectly, over the whole country. I consider this one of the chief causes of the maintenance of republican institutions in the United States. In cities it is impossible to prevent people from acting in concert and stirring one another into sudden and passionate resolutions. Cities may be regarded as large assemblies in which every inhabitant is a member. Their populace has an enormous influence on the magistrates, and often carries out its own wishes without their involvement.

a [ The United States has no metropolis, but it already contains several very large cities. In 1830 Philadelphia counted 161,000 inhabitants and New York 202,000. The lower classes who live in these cities form a rabble even more dangerous than the populace of European towns. They consist, first, of freed Black people, whom the laws and public opinion condemn to a hereditary state of misery and degradation. They also include a multitude of Europeans who have been driven to the shores of the New World by misfortune or misconduct. These men infect the United States with all our vices, and they bring with them none of the interests that might counteract their harmful influence. Because they live in a country where they have no civil rights, they are ready to turn every passion that stirs the community to their own advantage. Thus, within the last few months, serious riots have broken out in Philadelphia and in New York. Disturbances of this kind are unknown in the rest of the country, which is not at all alarmed by them, because the city population has so far had no power or influence over the rural districts. Nevertheless, I regard the size of certain American cities, and especially the nature of their population, as a real danger to the future security of the democratic republics of the New World. I venture to predict that they will perish from this cause, unless the government manages to create an armed force that will stay under the control of the national majority while remaining independent of the city population and able to put down its excesses.

[The population of the city of New York had risen, by 1870, to 942,292, and that of Philadelphia to 674,022. Brooklyn, which may be said to form part of New York City, has a population of 396,099 in addition to that of New York. The frequent disturbances in the great cities of America, and the excessive corruption of their local governments, over which there is no effective control, are among the greatest evils and dangers of the country.]]

To subject the provinces to the metropolis is therefore to do two things. It places the fate of the empire in the hands of one part of the community, which can be condemned as unjust. It also places it in the hands of a populace acting on its own impulses, which must be avoided as dangerous. The dominance of capital cities is therefore a serious blow to the representative system. It exposes modern republics to the same defect as the republics of antiquity, which all perished because they did not know that form of government.

I could easily list a great number of secondary causes that have helped establish the democratic republic of the United States and that help maintain it. But among these favorable elements I discern two principal ones, which I hasten to point out. I have already observed that the origin of the American settlements can be seen as the first and most effective cause to which the present prosperity of the United States may be attributed. The Americans had the chances of birth in their favor. Their forefathers brought with them into the country that equality of conditions from which the democratic republic has very naturally grown. Nor was this all they did. Besides this republican state of society, the early settlers handed down to their descendants the customs, mores, and opinions that contribute most to the success of a republican form of government. When I reflect on the consequences of this first circumstance, I seem to see the destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores, just as the whole human race was represented by the first man.

The chief circumstance that has favored the establishment and the maintenance of a democratic republic in the United States is the nature of the territory the Americans inhabit. Their ancestors gave them the love of equality and of freedom, but God himself gave them the means of remaining equal and free, by placing them on a boundless continent open to their efforts. General prosperity favors the stability of all governments, but especially of a democratic constitution. A democracy depends on the dispositions of the majority, and above all on that part of the community that is most exposed to the pressure of want. When the people rules, it must be made happy, or it will overturn the State. And misery can drive it to the same excesses to which ambition drives kings. The physical causes, independent of the laws, that help promote general prosperity are more numerous in America than they have ever been in any other country in the world, at any other time in history. In the United States, not only is the legislation democratic, but nature herself favors the cause of the people.

In what part of human tradition can we find anything similar to what is happening before our eyes in North America? The famous communities of antiquity were all founded among hostile nations, which they had to subjugate before they could flourish in their place. Even the moderns have found, in some parts of South America, vast regions inhabited by a people of inferior civilization, who nevertheless occupied and cultivated the soil. To found their new states, the settlers had to wipe out or subdue a numerous population, until civilization was made to blush for its success. But North America was inhabited only by wandering tribes, who gave no thought to the natural riches of the soil. That vast country was still, properly speaking, an empty continent, a desert land awaiting its inhabitants.

Everything is extraordinary in America, the social condition of the inhabitants as well as the laws. But the soil on which these institutions are founded is more extraordinary than all the rest. When the Creator first placed man on the earth, the earth was inexhaustible in its youth, but man was weak and ignorant. By the time he had learned to uncover the treasures it contained, hosts of his fellow creatures covered its surface, and he had to win a refuge of rest and freedom by the sword. At that very time North America was discovered, as if it had been kept in reserve by the Deity and had just risen from beneath the waters of the flood.

That continent still shows, as it did in the earliest times, rivers that rise from never-failing sources, green and moist solitudes, and fields that the farmer’s plow has never turned. In this state it is offered to man. It is offered not to man in the barbarous and isolated condition of the early ages, but to a being who already holds the most powerful secrets of the natural world, who is united with his fellow men, and who has been instructed by the experience of fifty centuries. At this very moment thirteen million civilized Europeans are peacefully spreading over those fertile plains, whose resources and extent they do not yet know accurately themselves. Three or four thousand soldiers drive the wandering Native American tribes before them. The pioneers follow the soldiers. They cut through the woods, scare off the beasts of prey, trace the courses of the inland streams, and prepare the triumphal march of civilization across the wilderness.

Others have so often described the favorable influence of America’s material prosperity on the institutions of that country, and I myself have so often mentioned it, that I shall not dwell on it beyond adding a few facts. People commonly hold a mistaken notion that the deserts of America are peopled by European emigrants who land every year on the coasts of the New World, while the American population grows and multiplies on the soil its forefathers tilled. In fact, the European settler usually arrives in the United States without friends, and sometimes without resources. To survive he has to work for hire, and he rarely goes beyond the belt of industrious population next to the ocean. The desert cannot be explored without capital or credit, and the body must be accustomed to the hardships of a new climate before it can be exposed to the risks of forest life. It is the Americans themselves who leave the places of their birth every day to acquire extensive lands in a remote country. Thus the European leaves his cottage for the shores across the Atlantic, and the American, who was born on that very coast, plunges in his turn into the wilds of Central America. This double emigration never stops. It begins in the remotest parts of Europe, it crosses the Atlantic Ocean, and it advances across the solitudes of the New World. Millions of men are marching at once toward the same horizon. Their language, their religion, and their customs differ, but their object is the same. The gifts of fortune are promised in the West, and to the West they turn their steps. *b

b [ [The number of foreign immigrants into the United States in the last fifty years (from 1820 to 1871) is stated to be 7,556,007. Of these, 4,104,553 spoke English—that is, they came from Great Britain, Ireland, or the British colonies; 2,643,069 came from Germany or northern Europe; and about half a million from the south of Europe.]]

Nothing can be compared with this continuous movement of the human race, except perhaps the invasions that preceded the fall of the Roman Empire. Then, as now, generations of men were driven forward in the same direction, to meet and struggle on the same ground. But the designs of Providence were not the same. Then, every newcomer was the herald of destruction and death. Now, every adventurer brings with him the elements of prosperity and life. The future still hides from us the further consequences of this westward migration of the Americans, but we can easily see its more immediate results. Every year a portion of the inhabitants leave the States where they were born. As a result, the population of those States grows very slowly, even though they were settled long ago. Thus in Connecticut, which has only fifty-nine inhabitants to the square mile, the population has not grown by more than one quarter in forty years, while that of England has grown by one third in the same period. The European emigrant therefore always lands in a country that is only half full, and where hands are in demand. He becomes a workman in comfortable circumstances. His son goes to seek his fortune in unsettled regions, and he becomes a rich landowner. The father accumulates the capital that the son invests, and neither the foreigner nor the native knows want.

The laws of the United States are extremely favorable to the division of property. But a cause more powerful than the laws prevents property from being divided to excess. *c This is easy to see in the States that are beginning to be thickly peopled. Massachusetts is the most populous part of the Union, yet it contains only eighty inhabitants to the square mile, which is much fewer than in France, where 162 are counted on the same area. But in Massachusetts estates are very rarely divided. The eldest son takes the land, and the others go to seek their fortune in the desert. The law has abolished the rights of primogeniture, but circumstances have combined to restore it in a form that no one can complain of, and that harms no just rights.
c [ In New England the estates are exceedingly small, but they are rarely subjected to further division.]

A single fact will be enough to show the enormous number of people who leave New England in this way to settle in the wilds. We were assured in 1830 that thirty-six members of Congress were born in the little State of Connecticut. The population of Connecticut, which makes up only one forty-third of that of the United States, thus supplied one eighth of the whole body of representatives. Yet the State of Connecticut itself sends only five delegates to Congress, and the thirty-one others sit for the new Western States. If these thirty-one men had remained in Connecticut, they would probably have remained humble laborers instead of becoming rich landowners. They would have lived in obscurity, unable to rise into public life. And far from becoming useful members of the legislature, they might have been unruly citizens.

These reflections do not escape the Americans any more than they escape us. “It cannot be doubted,” says Chancellor Kent in his “Treatise on American Law,” “that the division of landed estates must produce great evils when it is carried to such excess as that each parcel of land is insufficient to support a family; but these disadvantages have never been felt in the United States, and many generations must elapse before they can be felt. The extent of our inhabited territory, the abundance of adjacent land, and the continual stream of emigration flowing from the shores of the Atlantic towards the interior of the country, suffice as yet, and will long suffice, to prevent the parcelling out of estates.”

It is hard to describe the greed with which the American rushes forward to seize the immense prize that fortune holds out to him. In the chase he fearlessly faces the Native American’s arrow and the diseases of the forest. The silence of the woods does not impress him, and the approach of beasts of prey does not disturb him, for he is driven on by a passion more intense than the love of life. Before him lies a boundless continent, and he presses on as if time were short, and he were afraid of finding no room for his efforts. I have spoken of the emigration from the older States, but how shall I describe the emigration from the newer ones? Barely fifty years have passed since the State of Ohio was founded. Most of its inhabitants were not born within its borders. Its capital has been built only thirty years, and its territory is still covered by an immense stretch of uncultivated fields. Nevertheless the population of Ohio is already moving westward, and most of the settlers who go down into the fertile savannahs of Illinois are citizens of Ohio. These men left their first country to improve their condition, and they leave their new home to improve it still more. Fortune awaits them everywhere, but happiness they cannot reach. The desire for prosperity has become in their minds an ardent and restless passion that grows by what it gains. Early on, they broke the ties that bound them to their native soil, and they have formed no new ones along the way. Emigration was at first a necessity for them, a means of survival. It soon becomes a kind of game of chance, which they pursue as much for the excitement it brings as for the profit it yields.

Sometimes man’s progress is so rapid that the desert reappears behind him. The woods bend to make a passage for him, and spring up again when he has passed. In crossing the new States of the West, it is not unusual to come upon deserted dwellings in the middle of the wilds. The traveler often finds the remains of a log house in the most solitary retreats, and they bear witness to the power of man, and no less to his inconstancy. Over these abandoned fields and these ruins of a day, the primeval forest soon scatters fresh vegetation. The beasts return to the haunts that were once their own. And Nature covers the traces of man’s path with branches and flowers, which wipe out his fleeting track.

I remember that I was once crossing one of the wooded districts that still cover the State of New York, when I reached the shore of a lake set deep in forests as old as the world. A small island, covered with woods whose thick foliage hid its banks, rose from the middle of the water. On the shores of the lake nothing showed the presence of man, except a column of smoke on the horizon, rising from the treetops to the clouds. It seemed to hang from heaven rather than to climb toward the sky. A Native American boat had been hauled up on the sand, and it tempted me to visit the islet that had first caught my eye. In a few minutes I set foot on its banks. The whole island was one of those delightful solitudes of the New World that almost make civilized man regret the haunts of the savage. A luxuriant vegetation bore witness to the incomparable fruitfulness of the soil. The deep silence common to the wilds of North America was broken only by the hoarse cooing of the wood pigeon and the tapping of the woodpecker on the bark of the trees. I was far from supposing that this spot had ever been inhabited, so completely did Nature seem to have been left to her own whims. But when I reached the center of the island, I thought I discovered some traces of man. I then examined the surrounding objects with care, and I soon saw that a European had undoubtedly come to seek refuge in this retreat. Yet what changes had taken place in the scene of his labors! The logs he had hastily cut to build himself a shed had sprouted again. Even the props were intertwined with living greenery, and his cabin had become a bower. Among these shrubs a few stones could be seen, blackened with fire and sprinkled with thin ashes. Here the hearth had no doubt been, and the chimney, in falling, had covered it with rubble. For some time I stood in silent admiration of the exuberance of Nature and the littleness of man. And when I had to leave that enchanting solitude, I exclaimed sadly, “Are ruins, then, already here?”

In Europe we tend to regard a restless disposition, an unbounded desire for riches, and an excessive love of independence as tendencies very dangerous to society. Yet these are the very elements that ensure a long and peaceful life for the republics of America. Without these restless passions the population would gather in certain spots and would soon be subject to wants like those of the Old World, which are hard to satisfy. Such is the present good fortune of the New World that the vices of its inhabitants are scarcely less favorable to society than their virtues. These circumstances have a great influence on how human actions are judged in the two hemispheres. What we would call greed, the Americans often call praiseworthy industry. And they blame as faintheartedness what we regard as the virtue of moderate desires.

In France, simple tastes, orderly habits, domestic affections, and the attachment men feel to the place of their birth are regarded as great guarantees of the peace and happiness of the state. But in America nothing seems more harmful to society than these virtues. The French Canadians have faithfully preserved the traditions of their original customs, and they are already short of room on their small territory. This little community, which has only recently begun to exist, will soon fall prey to the calamities that afflict old nations. In Canada the most educated, patriotic, and humane inhabitants make extraordinary efforts to make the people dissatisfied with the simple enjoyments that still content them. There, the seductions of wealth are praised with as much zeal as the charms of an honest but limited income are praised in the Old World. More effort is spent there on exciting the passions of the citizens than elsewhere on calming them. If we listen to their praises, we shall hear that nothing is more admirable than to trade the pure and homely pleasures that even the poor man enjoys in his own country for the dull delights of prosperity under a foreign sky. We shall hear that it is admirable to leave the family hearth and the turf beneath which one’s forefathers sleep, in short, to abandon the living and the dead in search of fortune.

At present America offers a field for human effort far more extensive than any amount of labor that can be applied to work it. In America too much knowledge cannot be spread, for all knowledge, while it may serve the one who possesses it, also benefits those who do not. New wants are not to be feared, since they can be satisfied without difficulty. The growth of human passions need not be dreaded, since all passions can find an easy and legitimate object. Nor can men be given too much freedom, since they are scarcely ever tempted to misuse their liberties.

The American republics of today are like companies of adventurers formed to explore the wastelands of the New World together and to carry on a flourishing trade. The passions that stir the Americans most deeply are not political but commercial. Or, to put it more accurately, they bring the habits they form in business into their political life. They love order, without which business does not prosper, and they set a special value on regular conduct, which is the foundation of a solid business. They prefer the good sense that builds large fortunes to the enterprising spirit that so often squanders them. General ideas alarm their minds, which are used to positive calculations, and they hold practice in higher honor than theory.

It is in America that one learns to understand the influence that physical prosperity has on political actions, and even on opinions that ought to acknowledge no authority but reason. This truth is most visible among foreigners. Most of the European emigrants to the New World bring with them that wild love of independence and of change that our calamities so readily produce. I sometimes met Europeans in the United States who had been forced to leave their own country because of their political opinions. They all astonished me by what they said, but one of them surprised me more than all the rest. I was crossing one of the most remote districts of Pennsylvania when night overtook me, and I had to beg for hospitality at the gate of a wealthy planter, a Frenchman by birth. He asked me to sit down by his fire, and we began to talk with the freedom that suits people who meet in the backwoods, two thousand leagues from their native country. I knew that my host had been a great leveler and an ardent demagogue forty years earlier, and that his name was not unknown to fame. So I was more than a little surprised to hear him discuss the rights of property as an economist or a landowner might have done. He spoke of the necessary gradations that fortune establishes among men, of obedience to established laws, of the influence of good morals in commonwealths, and of the support that religious opinions give to order and to freedom. He even went so far as to quote an evangelical authority in support of one of his political tenets.

I listened, and I marveled at the weakness of human reason. A proposition is true or false, but amid the uncertainties of science and the conflicting lessons of experience, no art can prove it to be one or the other until some new event clears away the clouds of doubt. I was poor, and I become rich. I should not expect prosperity to act on my conduct and leave my judgment free. My opinions change with my fortune, and the happy circumstances I turn to my advantage supply the decisive argument that was missing before. The influence of prosperity acts even more freely on the American than on foreigners. The American has always seen public order and public prosperity, intimately united as they are, advance together before his eyes. He cannot conceive that one can exist without the other. He therefore has nothing to forget, and he has no need, like so many Europeans, to unlearn the lessons of his early education.
Influence of the Laws on the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States
Three principal causes of the maintenance of the democratic republic — Federal Constitutions — Municipal institutions — Judicial power.

The principal aim of this book has been to make the laws of the United States known. If this purpose has been accomplished, the reader is already able to judge for himself which laws really tend to maintain the democratic republic and which ones endanger its existence. If I have not succeeded in explaining this over the whole course of my work, I cannot hope to do so within the limits of a single chapter. I do not intend to retrace the path I have already followed, and a very few lines will be enough to sum up what I have already explained.
Three circumstances seem to me to contribute most powerfully to the maintenance of the democratic republic in the United States.
The first is the Federal system of government that the Americans have adopted. It allows the Union to have the power of a great empire together with the security of a small State.
The second consists in the municipal institutions that limit the despotism of the majority, and at the same time give the people a taste for freedom and a knowledge of the art of being free.

The third lies in how the judicial power is constituted. I have shown how the courts of justice help hold back the excesses of democracy, and how they restrain and steer the impulses of the majority without halting its activity.
Influence of Manners on the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States

I have remarked before that the manners of the people may be considered one of the general causes to which the maintenance of a democratic republic in the United States is due. Here I used the word manners in the sense the ancients gave to the word mores. I apply it not only to manners in the proper sense, that is, what makes up the character of social intercourse. I extend it to the various notions and opinions current among men, and to the mass of ideas that form their cast of mind. I therefore include under this term the whole moral and intellectual condition of a people. My intention is not to draw a picture of American manners. It is simply to point out those features of them that favor the maintenance of political institutions.
Religion Considered as a Political Institution, Which Powerfully Contributes to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic Among the Americans

North America peopled by men who professed a democratic and republican Christianity—Arrival of the Catholics—Why the Catholics form the most democratic and the most republican class at the present time.

Every religion is found alongside a political opinion connected to it by affinity. If the human mind is left to follow its own bent, it will regulate the temporal and spiritual institutions of society on one uniform principle. Man will try, if I may use the expression, to bring the state in which he lives on earth into harmony with the state that he believes awaits him in heaven. Most of British America was peopled by men who had shaken off the authority of the Pope and acknowledged no other religious supremacy. They brought with them into the New World a form of Christianity that I cannot describe better than by calling it a democratic and republican religion. This sect contributed powerfully to the establishment of a democracy and a republic. From the earliest settlement of the emigrants, politics and religion formed an alliance that has never been dissolved.

About fifty years ago Ireland began to pour a Catholic population into the United States. On the other side, the Catholics of America made converts, and at present more than a million Christians professing the truths of the Church of Rome are to be found in the Union. *d The Catholics are faithful to the observances of their religion, and they are fervent and zealous in believing and defending its doctrines. Nevertheless they form the most republican and the most democratic class of citizens in the United States. This fact may surprise the observer at first, but on reflection the causes behind it are easy to discover.

d [ [It is difficult to ascertain accurately the size of the Roman Catholic population of the United States, but in 1868 an able writer in the “Edinburgh Review” (vol. cxxvii. p. 521) affirmed that the whole Catholic population of the United States was then about 4,000,000, divided into 43 dioceses, with 3,795 churches, under the care of 45 bishops and 2,317 clergymen. But this rapid increase is mainly supported by immigration from the Catholic countries of Europe.]]

I think people have been wrong to regard the Catholic religion as the natural enemy of democracy. Among the various Christian sects, Catholicism seems to me, on the contrary, to be one of the most favorable to the equality of conditions. The Catholic Church has only two elements in its religious community: the priest and the people. Only the priest stands above the rank of his flock, and everyone below him is equal.

On points of doctrine the Catholic faith places all human capacities on the same level. It subjects the wise and the ignorant, the man of genius and the common crowd, to the details of the same creed. It imposes the same observances on the rich and the poor, and inflicts the same austerities on the strong and the weak. It accepts no compromise with mortal man. It reduces the whole human race to the same standard, and it merges all the distinctions of society at the foot of the same altar, just as they are merged in the sight of God. Catholicism may dispose the faithful to obedience, but it certainly does not prepare them for inequality. The opposite may be said of Protestantism, which generally tends to make men independent more than to make them equal.

Catholicism is like an absolute monarchy. If the sovereign is removed, all the other classes of society are more equal than they are in republics. It has not infrequently happened that the Catholic priest has left the service of the altar to join the governing powers of society and take his place among the civil ranks of men. This religious influence has sometimes been used to secure the interests of the political order to which he belonged. At other times Catholics have taken the side of aristocracy out of a spirit of religion.

But as soon as the priesthood is entirely separated from the government, as it is in the United States, no class of men is found more naturally disposed than the Catholics to carry the doctrine of the equality of conditions into the political world. If, then, the Catholic citizens of the United States are not forcibly led by the nature of their beliefs to adopt democratic and republican principles, at least they are not necessarily opposed to them. And their social position, as well as their small numbers, obliges them to adopt these opinions. Most of the Catholics are poor, and they have no chance of taking part in the government unless it is open to all citizens. They are a minority, and all rights must be respected in order to secure them the free exercise of their own privileges. These two causes lead them, without their knowing it, to adopt political doctrines that they would perhaps support with less zeal if they were rich and dominant.

The Catholic clergy of the United States has never tried to resist this political tendency. Instead it works to justify what follows from it. The priests in America have divided the intellectual world into two parts. In one they place the doctrines of revealed religion, which command their assent. In the other they leave those truths that they believe have been freely left open to political inquiry. Thus the Catholics of the United States are at the same time the most faithful believers and the most zealous citizens.

It may be said that in the United States no religious doctrine shows the slightest hostility to democratic and republican institutions. The clergy of all the different sects speak the same language, their opinions agree with the laws, and the human intellect flows onward in one single current.

I happened to be staying in one of the largest towns in the Union when I was invited to attend a public meeting. It had been called to help the Poles and to send them supplies of arms and money. I found two or three thousand people gathered in a vast hall that had been prepared to receive them. After a short time a priest in his ecclesiastical robes stepped to the front of the platform. The spectators rose and stood with their heads uncovered while he spoke in the following terms:—

“Almighty God! the God of Armies! Thou who didst strengthen the hearts and guide the arms of our fathers when they were fighting for the sacred rights of national independence; Thou who didst make them triumph over a hateful oppression, and hast granted to our people the benefits of liberty and peace; Turn, O Lord, a favorable eye upon the other hemisphere; pitifully look down upon that heroic nation which is even now struggling as we did in the former time, and for the same rights which we defended with our blood. Thou, who didst create Man in the likeness of the same image, let not tyranny mar Thy work, and establish inequality upon the earth. Almighty God! do Thou watch over the destiny of the Poles, and render them worthy to be free. May Thy wisdom direct their councils, and may Thy strength sustain their arms! Shed forth Thy terror over their enemies, scatter the powers which take counsel against them; and vouchsafe that the injustice which the world has witnessed for fifty years, be not consummated in our time. O Lord, who holdest alike the hearts of nations and of men in Thy powerful hand; raise up allies to the sacred cause of right; arouse the French nation from the apathy in which its rulers retain it, that it go forth again to fight for the liberties of the world.

“Lord, turn not Thou Thy face from us, and grant that we may always be the most religious as well as the freest people of the earth. Almighty God, hear our supplications this day. Save the Poles, we beseech Thee, in the name of Thy well-beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who died upon the cross for the salvation of men. Amen.”
The whole meeting answered “Amen!” with devotion.
Indirect Influence of Religious Opinions on Political Society in the United States

Christian morality common to all sects — Influence of religion on the customs of the Americans — Respect for the marriage tie — How religion confines the imagination of the Americans within certain limits and checks the passion for innovation — The Americans’ opinion of the political usefulness of religion — Their efforts to extend and secure its predominance.

I have just shown what direct influence religion has on politics in the United States. Its indirect influence, however, seems to me even greater, and it never teaches the Americans more fully the art of being free than when it says nothing about freedom.

The sects in the United States are innumerable. They all differ about the worship that man owes his Creator, but they all agree about the duties that people owe one another. Each sect worships God in its own way, but all of them preach the same moral law in God’s name. For an individual, it is of the highest importance that his religion be true, but society is in a different position. Society has no future life to hope for or to fear, and as long as the citizens profess a religion, the particular tenets of that religion matter very little to its interests. Moreover, almost all the sects of the United States belong to the great unity of Christianity, and Christian morality is the same everywhere.

It may fairly be believed that a certain number of Americans follow a particular form of worship more from habit than from conviction. In the United States the sovereign authority is religious, and so hypocrisy must be common. Yet there is no country in the world where the Christian religion keeps a greater hold on the souls of men than in America. And there can be no greater proof of its usefulness, and of its conformity to human nature, than that its influence is felt most powerfully in the most educated and free nation on earth.

I have observed that the American clergy in general, without even excepting those who do not accept religious liberty, all favor civil freedom, but they do not support any particular political system. They keep aloof from parties and from public affairs. In the United States religion has little influence on the laws or on the details of public opinion, but it directs the customs of the community, and by regulating domestic life it regulates the state.

I have no doubt that the great austerity of customs observable in the United States arises, in the first place, from religious faith. Religion often cannot restrain man from the countless temptations of fortune, nor can it check the passion for gain that every incident of his life helps to arouse. But its influence over the mind of woman is supreme, and women are the guardians of morals. There is certainly no country in the world where the marriage tie is so much respected as in America, or where conjugal happiness is more highly or more justly valued. In Europe almost all the disturbances of society arise from irregularities in domestic life. To despise the natural bonds and legitimate pleasures of home is to acquire a taste for excess, a restlessness of heart, and the evil of shifting desires. Stirred by the tumultuous passions that so often disturb his household, the European chafes at the obedience that the legislative powers of the state demand of him. But when the American withdraws from the turmoil of public life to the bosom of his family, he finds there the image of order and peace. There his pleasures are simple and natural, his joys innocent and calm. Since he finds that an orderly life is the surest path to happiness, he easily accustoms himself to moderating his opinions as well as his tastes. While the European tries to forget his domestic troubles by stirring up society, the American draws from his own home the love of order that he afterward carries into public affairs.

In the United States the influence of religion is not confined to customs; it extends to the intelligence of the people. Among the Anglo-Americans, some profess the doctrines of Christianity out of sincere belief, and others do so because they are afraid of being suspected of unbelief. Christianity therefore reigns without any obstacle, by universal consent. The consequence, as I have observed before, is that every principle of the moral world is fixed and settled, although the political world is left to the debates and experiments of men. Thus the human mind is never left to wander across a boundless field, and whatever its pretensions, it is checked from time to time by barriers it cannot get past. Before it can innovate, certain primary and unchangeable principles are laid down, and the boldest conceptions of human invention are subjected to certain forms that slow down and halt their completion.

The imagination of the Americans, even in its greatest flights, is cautious and hesitant; its impulses are held in check and its works left unfinished. These habits of restraint recur in political society, and they are remarkably favorable both to the tranquility of the people and to the durability of the institutions they have established. Nature and circumstances combined to make the inhabitants of the United States bold men, as the enterprising spirit with which they pursue fortune amply shows. If the American mind were free of all constraints, the Americans would very soon become the most daring innovators and the most relentless disputants in the world. But the revolutionaries of America are obliged to profess an outward respect for Christian morality and equity, which does not easily allow them to violate the laws that stand in the way of their designs. Nor would they find it easy to overcome the scruples of their followers, even if they could get past their own. Up to now no one in the United States has dared to put forward the maxim that everything is permissible in the interest of society. It is an impious adage, which seems to have been invented in an age of freedom to shelter all the tyrants of future ages. Thus, while the law allows the Americans to do whatever they please, religion keeps them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, whatever is rash or unjust.

Religion in America takes no direct part in the government of society, but it must nonetheless be regarded as the first of the political institutions of that country. For even if it does not give Americans a taste for freedom, it makes the use of free institutions easier. Indeed, this is the very point of view from which the inhabitants of the United States themselves look at religious belief. I do not know whether all the Americans have a sincere faith in their religion, for who can search the human heart? But I am certain that they hold it to be indispensable to the maintenance of republican institutions. This opinion does not belong to one class of citizens or to one party; it belongs to the whole nation and to every rank of society.

In the United States, if a political figure attacks one sect, that may not stop even the followers of that very sect from supporting him. But if he attacks all the sects together, everyone abandons him, and he is left alone.

While I was in America, a witness who happened to be called at the assizes of Chester County (State of New York) declared that he did not believe in the existence of God or in the immortality of the soul. The judge refused to admit his testimony, on the ground that the witness had destroyed in advance all the court’s confidence in what he was about to say. *e The newspapers reported the fact without any further comment.

e [ The New York “Spectator” of August 23, 1831, reports the fact in these terms: “The Court of Common Pleas of Chester county (New York) a few days since rejected a witness who declared his disbelief in the existence of God. The presiding judge remarked that he had not before been aware that there was a man living who did not believe in the existence of God; that this belief constituted the sanction of all testimony in a court of justice, and that he knew of no cause in a Christian country where a witness had been permitted to testify without such belief.”]

The Americans combine the ideas of Christianity and liberty so closely in their minds that it is impossible to make them conceive of one without the other. And with them this conviction does not spring from that barren, inherited faith that seems to vegetate in the soul rather than to live.

I know of societies that Americans have formed to send ministers of the Gospel into the new Western States, to found schools and churches there. They fear that religion might die out in those distant settlements, and that the young States might be less prepared for free institutions than the people they came from. I met wealthy New Englanders who had left the land of their birth to lay the foundations of Christianity and freedom on the banks of the Missouri or on the prairies of Illinois. In this way, the duties of patriotism keep religious zeal constantly alive in the United States. These men are not moved only by the promises of a future life. Eternity is just one of their reasons for devotion to the cause. And if you talk with these missionaries of Christian civilization, you will be surprised at how highly they value the goods of this world, and you will find a politician where you expected a priest. They will tell you that “all the American republics are collectively involved with each other; if the republics of the West were to fall into anarchy, or to be mastered by a despot, the republican institutions which now flourish upon the shores of the Atlantic Ocean would be in great peril. It is, therefore, our interest that the new States should be religious, in order to maintain our liberties.”

That is what the Americans think. Some people may claim that the religious spirit I admire is the worst fault in America, and that human freedom and happiness need only one more thing: belief in some blind account of creation, or the claim, with Cabanis, that the brain secretes thought. To them I can only answer that they have never been to America, and that they have never seen a religious nation or a free one. When they come back from their expedition, we will listen to what they have to say.

There are people in France who look on republican institutions as a temporary means to power, wealth, and distinction. They are the condottieri of liberty, who fight for their own advantage, whatever colors they wear. It is not to them that I am speaking. But there are others who look forward to the republican form of government as a calm and lasting state, toward which modern society is pushed more each day by the ideas and customs of the time, and who sincerely wish to prepare men to be free. When these men attack religious opinions, they obey the dictates of their passions to the harm of their own interests. Despotism may govern without faith, but liberty cannot. Religion is far more necessary in the republic they portray in glowing colors than in the monarchy they attack, and it is more needed in democratic republics than in any others. How can society escape destruction if the moral tie is not strengthened in proportion as the political tie is loosened? And what can be done with a people that is its own master, if it is not submissive to the Divinity?

Principal Causes That Make Religion Powerful in America Care the Americans take to separate the Church from the State — The laws, public opinion, and even the efforts of the clergy combine to promote this end — Influence of religion on the mind in the United States attributable to this cause — The reason for this — What the natural state of men is with regard to religion at the present time — What particular and incidental causes keep men, in certain countries, from reaching this state.

The philosophers of the eighteenth century explained the gradual decline of religious faith in a very simple way. Religious zeal, they said, must inevitably fade as liberty becomes more widely established and knowledge more widely spread. Unfortunately, the facts do not match their theory at all. There are certain populations in Europe whose unbelief is equaled only by their ignorance and degradation, while in America one of the freest and most educated nations in the world carries out all the outward duties of religious fervor.

When I arrived in the United States, the religious aspect of the country was the first thing that struck me. The longer I stayed, the more I saw the great political consequences that flowed from this state of things, to which I was unaccustomed. In France I had almost always seen the spirit of religion and the spirit of freedom pulling in directly opposite directions. In America I found them closely united, reigning together over the same country. My desire to discover the causes of this phenomenon grew from day to day. To satisfy it, I questioned the members of all the different sects. I sought out especially the company of the clergy, who are the keepers of the different persuasions and who have the greatest interest in their survival. As a member of the Roman Catholic Church, I was brought into particular contact with several of its priests, with whom I became closely acquainted. To each of these men I expressed my astonishment and explained my doubts. I found that they differed only on matters of detail, and that they mainly attributed the peaceful dominion of religion in their country to the separation of Church and State. I do not hesitate to affirm that during my stay in America I did not meet a single person, of the clergy or of the laity, who was not of the same opinion on this point.

This led me to examine more closely than I had before the place the American clergy hold in political society. I learned with surprise that they hold no public appointments. *f Not one of them is to be found in the administration, and they are not even represented in the legislative assemblies. In several States *g the law excludes them from political life, and public opinion does so in all. And when I came to inquire into the prevailing spirit of the clergy, I found that most of them seemed to withdraw of their own accord from the exercise of power, and that they made it a point of pride in their profession to stay out of politics.

I heard them denounce ambition and deceit, whatever political opinions these vices might happen to lurk beneath. But I learned from what they said that men are not guilty in the eyes of God for any opinions about political government that they may sincerely profess, any more than for their mistakes in building a house or plowing a furrow. I saw that these ministers of the gospel avoided all parties with the care that people show for their own personal interest. These facts convinced me that what I had been told was true. It then became my aim to investigate the causes, and to ask how it happened that the real authority of religion was increased by a state of things that reduced its apparent strength. These causes did not long escape my inquiries.

The short span of sixty years can never satisfy the imagination of man, nor can the imperfect joys of this world satisfy his heart. Man alone, of all created beings, shows a natural contempt for existence and yet a boundless desire to exist. He scorns life, but he dreads annihilation. These conflicting feelings constantly drive his soul to contemplate a future state, and religion directs his thoughts there. Religion, then, is simply another form of hope, and it is no less natural to the human heart than hope itself. Men cannot abandon their religious faith without a kind of mental aberration and a sort of violent distortion of their true nature. But they are irresistibly brought back to more devout feelings, for unbelief is an accident, and faith is the only permanent state of mankind. If we consider religious institutions from a purely human point of view, we may say that they draw an inexhaustible source of strength from man himself, since they belong to one of the constituent principles of human nature.

I am aware that at certain times religion may reinforce this influence, which originates in itself, with the artificial power of the laws and the support of the temporal institutions that direct society. Religions closely united to the governments of the earth have been known to exercise a sovereign authority drawn from the twofold source of terror and faith. But when a religion enters into an alliance of this kind, I do not hesitate to affirm that it makes the same mistake as a man who would sacrifice his future to his present welfare. In gaining a power to which it has no claim, it puts at risk the authority that is rightfully its own. When a religion founds its empire on the desire for immortality that lives in every human heart, it may aspire to universal dominion. But when it attaches itself to a government, it must necessarily adopt maxims that apply only to certain nations. Thus, by forming an alliance with a political power, religion increases its authority over a few and gives up the hope of reigning over all.

As long as a religion rests on those feelings that console every affliction, it can win the affections of mankind. But if it becomes mixed up with the bitter passions of the world, it may be forced to defend allies given to it by its interests and not by the principle of love, or to repel as enemies men who are still attached to its spirit, however opposed they may be to the powers with which it is allied. The Church cannot share the temporal power of the state without becoming the object of some of the animosity that the state arouses.

The political powers that seem most firmly established often have no better guarantee of their duration than the opinions of a generation, the interests of the time, or the life of one individual. A law can change the social condition that seems most fixed and settled, and when the social condition changes, everything else must change with it. The powers of society are more or less fleeting, like the years we spend on earth. They follow one another rapidly, like the passing cares of life, and no government has ever yet been founded on an unchanging disposition of the human heart or on an imperishable interest.

As long as a religion is sustained by those feelings, tendencies, and passions that occur in the same forms in every period of history, it can defy the efforts of time. At the least, it can be destroyed only by another religion. But when religion clings to the interests of the world, it becomes almost as fragile as the powers of the earth. It is the only one of them all that can hope for immortality. But if it is tied to their ephemeral authority, it shares their fortunes, and may fall along with the transient passions that supported them for a day. The alliance that religion makes with political powers must be burdensome to itself, since it does not need their help to live, and by giving them its help it may expose itself to decay.

The danger I have just pointed out always exists, but it is not always equally visible. In some ages governments seem imperishable; in others, the existence of society seems more precarious than the life of a man. Some constitutions plunge the citizens into a lethargic drowsiness, and others rouse them to feverish excitement. When governments seem so strong and laws so stable, men do not see the dangers that may arise from a union of Church and State. When governments show so much weakness and laws so much inconstancy, the danger is obvious, but by then it can no longer be avoided. To be effective, measures must be taken to detect its approach.

The more a nation takes on a democratic social condition, and the more communities show democratic tendencies, the more dangerous it becomes to connect religion with political institutions. For the time is coming when authority will be tossed from hand to hand, when political theories will succeed one another, and when men, laws, and constitutions will disappear or be modified from day to day, and this not for a season only but unceasingly. Agitation and instability are inherent in the nature of democratic republics, just as stagnation and inertia are the law of absolute monarchies.

The Americans change the head of the government once in four years, elect new legislators every two years, and renew the provincial officers every twelve months. They have abandoned the political world to the attempts of innovators. If they had not placed religion beyond the innovators’ reach, where could it abide in the ebb and flow of human opinions? Where would the respect that belongs to it be paid, amid the struggles of faction? And what would become of its immortality, in the midst of perpetual decay? The American clergy were the first to see this truth and to act on it. They saw that they must give up their religious influence if they were to strive for political power, and they chose to give up the support of the state rather than share its changing fortunes.

Perhaps religion in America has less power than it has held at certain times among certain peoples, but its influence lasts longer. It relies only on its own resources, and no one can take those away. It operates within a narrow circle of principles, yet those principles belong wholly to it, and nobody disputes its authority over them.

On every side in Europe we hear voices complaining of the absence of religious faith and asking how to restore to religion some remnant of its original authority. It seems to me that we must first consider carefully what ought to be the natural state of men with regard to religion at the present time. When we know what we have to hope and to fear, we may see the end toward which our efforts ought to be directed.

The two great dangers that threaten the existence of religions are schism and indifference. In ages of fervent devotion, men sometimes abandon their religion, but they shake it off only in order to adopt another. Their faith changes its objects, but it suffers no decline. The old religion then arouses enthusiastic attachment or bitter enmity on either side. Some leave it in anger, others cling to it with increased devotion, and although persuasions differ, irreligion is unknown. This is not the case, however, when a religious belief is secretly undermined by doctrines that may be called negative, since they deny the truth of one religion without affirming that of any other. Prodigious revolutions then take place in the human mind, without the apparent cooperation of human passions and almost without man’s knowledge. Men lose the objects of their fondest hopes as if through forgetfulness. They are carried away by an imperceptible current that they lack the courage to resist, but which they follow with regret, since it bears them from a faith they love to a skepticism that plunges them into despair.

In ages that fit this description, men desert their religious opinions out of lukewarmness rather than dislike. They do not reject them, but the feelings that once sustained them disappear. Yet although the unbeliever does not admit religion to be true, he still considers it useful. Looking at religious institutions from a human point of view, he acknowledges their influence on customs and on legislation. He admits that they may help men live in peace with one another and prepare them gently for the hour of death. He regrets the faith he has lost. Since he has been deprived of a treasure whose full value he has learned to recognize, he hesitates to take it from those who still possess it.

On the other hand, those who continue to believe are not afraid to avow their faith openly. They look on those who do not share their persuasion as more deserving of pity than of opposition, and they know that to win the esteem of unbelievers they need not follow their example. They are hostile to no one in the world. They do not consider the society in which they live as an arena in which religion is bound to face its thousand deadly foes, and so they love their contemporaries while they condemn their weaknesses and lament their errors.

Since those who do not believe conceal their unbelief, and those who believe display their faith, public opinion declares itself in favor of religion. Love, support, and honor are bestowed on it, and only by searching the human soul can we detect the wounds it has received. The mass of mankind, who are never without a religious feeling, see nothing at odds with the established faith. The instinctive desire for a future life brings the crowd to the altar and opens men’s hearts to the precepts and consolations of religion.

But this picture does not apply to us. Among us there are men who have ceased to believe in Christianity without adopting any other religion; others who are in the perplexities of doubt and who already pretend not to believe; and still others who are afraid to avow the Christian faith that they secretly cherish.

Amid these lukewarm partisans and ardent opponents there exists a small number of believers who are ready to brave all obstacles and to scorn all dangers in defense of their faith. They have done violence to human weakness in order to rise above public opinion. Excited by the effort they have made, they scarcely know where to stop. They know that the first use the French made of independence was to attack religion, so they look on their contemporaries with dread and recoil in alarm from the liberty their fellow citizens are seeking to obtain. Because unbelief appears to them a novelty, they include everything new in one indiscriminate hostility. They are at war with their age and country, and they regard every opinion put forward there as the necessary enemy of the faith.

Men today are not naturally in this condition with regard to religion. Some extraordinary or accidental cause must be at work in France, preventing the human mind from following its original tendencies and pushing it past the point where it would naturally stop. I am profoundly convinced that this extraordinary and accidental cause is the close tie between politics and religion. Europe’s unbelievers attack Christians as their political opponents rather than as their religious adversaries. They hate the Christian religion as the opinion of a party far more than as a mistaken belief, and they reject the clergy less because the clergy are the representatives of the Divinity than because they are the allies of authority.

In Europe, Christianity has been closely united to the powers of the earth. Those powers are now in decay, and Christianity is, as it were, buried under their ruins. The living body of religion has been bound to the dead corpse of an outworn political order. Cut the bonds that hold it, and what is alive will rise once more. I do not know what could restore the Christian Church of Europe to the energy of its earlier days. That power belongs to God alone. But it may be within the reach of human policy to leave the faith free to exercise the full strength that it still retains.
How the Instruction, the Habits, and the Practical Experience of the Americans Promote the Success of Their Democratic Institutions

What is meant by the education of the American people — The human mind more superficially educated in the United States than in Europe — No one completely uneducated — The reason for this — How quickly opinions spread even in the uncultivated States of the West — Practical experience more useful to the Americans than book learning.
I have very little to add to what I have already said about the influence that the education and habits of the Americans have on the maintenance of their political institutions.

America has so far produced very few distinguished writers. It has no great historians and not a single eminent poet. Its inhabitants regard what are properly called literary pursuits with a kind of disapproval, and there are towns of quite secondary importance in Europe that publish more literary works each year than the twenty-four States of the Union put together. The Americans’ cast of mind is averse to general ideas, and it does not seek theoretical discoveries. Neither politics nor manufacturing directs them to such pursuits. And although new laws are constantly being enacted in the United States, no great writers have yet inquired into the general principles of their legislation. The Americans have lawyers and commentators but no jurists, *h and they offer the world examples rather than lessons. The same observation applies to the mechanical arts. In America the inventions of Europe are adopted with shrewdness; they are perfected and adapted with admirable skill to the needs of the country. Manufactures exist, but the science of manufacturing is not cultivated, and the Americans have good workmen but very few inventors. Fulton had to offer his services to foreign nations for a long time before he was able to devote them to his own country.
h [ [This cannot truthfully be said of the country of Kent, Story, and Wheaton.]]

An observer who wants to form an opinion about the state of education among the Anglo-Americans must look at the same subject from two different points of view. If he singles out only the learned, he will be astonished to find how rare they are. But if he counts the ignorant, the American people will appear to be the most educated community in the world. The whole population, as I observed elsewhere, lies between these two extremes. In New England every citizen receives the basics of human knowledge. He is also taught the doctrines and evidences of his religion, the history of his country, and the leading features of its Constitution. In the States of Connecticut and Massachusetts it is extremely rare to find a man imperfectly acquainted with all these things, and a person wholly ignorant of them is a kind of phenomenon.

When I compare the Greek and Roman republics with these American States — the manuscript libraries of the former and their rude population with the innumerable journals and the educated people of the latter — and when I recall all the attempts that are made to judge the modern republics by the help of those of antiquity, and to infer what will happen in our time from what took place two thousand years ago, I am tempted to burn my books so that I may apply only new ideas to so new a condition of society.

What I have said of New England must not, however, be applied indiscriminately to the whole Union. As we advance toward the West or the South, the education of the people declines. In the States bordering the Gulf of Mexico, a certain number of individuals may be found, as in our own countries, who lack the rudiments of education. But there is not a single district in the United States sunk in complete ignorance, and for a very simple reason. The peoples of Europe started from the darkness of a barbarous condition to advance toward the light of civilization. Their progress has been unequal: some of them have improved rapidly, while others have lingered on the way, and some have stopped and are still sleeping beside it. *i

i [ [In the Northern States the number of people with no education is small, the largest being 241,152 in the State of New York (according to Spaulding’s “Handbook of American Statistics” for 1874). But in the South no fewer than 1,516,339 whites and 2,671,396 Black people are returned as “illiterate.”]]

This has not been the case in the United States. The Anglo-Americans settled in a state of civilization on the territory their descendants now occupy. They did not have to begin to learn; it was enough for them not to forget. Now the children of these same Americans are the people who, year by year, move their dwellings into the wilds, and with their dwellings they carry their acquired knowledge and their esteem for learning. Education has taught them the usefulness of instruction and has enabled them to pass that instruction on to their children. In the United States society has no infancy; it is born grown up.

The Americans never use the word “peasant,” because they have no idea of the distinct class that the word describes. The ignorance of earlier ages, the simplicity of country life, and the rustic manners of the villager have not survived among them. They are equally strangers to the virtues, the vices, the coarse habits, and the simple graces of an early stage of civilization. At the far borders of the Confederate States, where society meets the wilderness, a population of bold adventurers has settled. They push into the solitude of the American forests and look for a new country there, to escape the poverty that awaited them in their native provinces. As soon as the pioneer reaches the spot that is to be his refuge, he fells a few trees and builds a log house. Nothing could look more wretched than these isolated dwellings. A traveler who approaches one of them toward nightfall sees the flicker of the hearth fire through the chinks in the walls. At night, if the wind rises, he hears the roof of boughs shaking to and fro among the great forest trees. Who would not take this poor hut for a refuge of crudeness and ignorance? Yet no comparison can be drawn between the pioneer and the dwelling that shelters him. Everything around him is primitive and unformed, but he himself is the product of the labor and experience of eighteen centuries. He dresses and speaks like the people of the cities. He knows the past, is curious about the future, and is ready to argue about the present. In short, he is a highly civilized man who agrees, for a time, to live in the backwoods, and who enters the wilds of the New World with a Bible, an axe, and a bundle of newspapers.

It is hard to imagine the incredible speed with which public opinion travels in the middle of these deserts. *j I do not think that so much intellectual exchange takes place even in the most educated and populous districts of France. *k There can be no doubt that, in the United States, the education of the people contributes powerfully to the support of a democratic republic. I believe this must always be so where education that awakens the understanding is not separated from moral training that improves the heart. But I do not exaggerate this benefit at all, and I am even further from thinking, as so many people in Europe do, that men can be turned into citizens at once by teaching them to read and write. True knowledge comes mainly from experience. If the Americans had not been gradually accustomed to governing themselves, their book learning would not help them much today.
